title: What are the whistleblowing requirements for firms in the DIFC?
description: DIFC whistleblowing: Regulatory Law Article 68A protection, DFSA GEN 5.4 policy and record rules, Employment Law victimization limits, and what to train.
shortAnswer: In the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), Article 68A of the Regulatory Law 2004 protects anyone who reports, in good faith, a reasonable suspicion of a DFSA rule breach, money laundering, fraud or other financial crime. DFSA General Module section 5.4 requires Authorised Persons to keep written whistleblowing policies, review them periodically, record every report, and inform officers and employees of the Article 68A protection. There is no prescribed training course.
keyTakeaways: Article 68A of the Regulatory Law protects whistleblowers from civil and contractual liability and from dismissal or detriment, and allows anonymous reports (Article 68A(6)).

GEN Rule 5.4.2 requires an Authorised Person to have appropriate and effective written policies and procedures to facilitate reporting and to assess and escalate concerns, and to review them periodically.
GEN Rule 5.4.3 requires a written record of each concern reported and the outcome of its assessment; the guidance lists seven items the record should include.
Guidance 9 under GEN 5.4.3 says firms should inform officers and employees of the Article 68A protection, which is the clearest training-related expectation in the regime.
The DIFC Employment Law's victimization protection in Article 60 covers acts connected with discrimination claims under Part 9, not financial whistleblowing generally.
jurisdiction: United Arab Emirates: Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC)
regulator: Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA) for the Regulatory Law and Rules; DIFC Authority (DIFCA) for the Employment Law
appliesTo: Authorised Persons regulated by the DFSA, which must meet the GEN 5.4 Rules
Regulated Entities and their officers and employees, whose suspected misconduct can be the subject of a protected disclosure under Article 68A
Any person making a disclosure, including current or former officers, employees, agents, service providers, and people with no formal connection to the firm (GEN 5.4.3 Guidance 7)
All DIFC employers and employees under the DIFC Employment Law for victimization and discrimination protections

sections.heading: Which laws govern whistleblowing in the DIFC?

blocks.text: Whistleblowing in the DIFC rests on two financial services instruments and one employment law. The DIFC is a financial free zone in Dubai with its own civil and commercial laws and its own financial regulator, the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), which administers the Regulatory Law 2004 and makes Rules under it, as described on the [DFSA legislation page](https://www.dfsa.ae/laws-rules/legal-resources/legislation).

items: **Regulatory Law 2004, Article 68A:** statutory protection for whistleblowers.
**DFSA General Module (GEN) section 5.4:** firm-level duties to have policies, procedures and records, made by Rule-making Instrument RMI318/2021 on October 27, 2021.

**DIFC Employment Law, DIFC Law No. 2 of 2019:** general employer duties, liability for employees' discrimination and victimization, and a victimization prohibition tied to its non-discrimination Part 9.

blocks.text: Onshore UAE and the Abu Dhabi Global Market have separate regimes, and a group with entities in more than one may need more than one policy. The [cross-country comparison of whistleblower training](/compare/whistleblower-training-requirements-by-country) shows how the DIFC sits alongside the EU, Australian, Japanese and US models.

sections.heading: Who is protected under Article 68A, and for what?

blocks.text: [Article 68A](https://dfsaen.thomsonreuters.com/rulebook/68a-whistleblower-protection) protects a person who discloses information about a reasonable suspicion that a Regulated Entity, its officers or employees, or, for an Authorised Person, an Affiliate or its officers or employees, has or may have contravened DFSA-administered legislation or "engaged in money laundering, fraud or any other financial crime". The disclosure must be made in good faith.

Article 68A(3) lists who can receive a protected disclosure: the Regulated Entity, its officers, a person performing a Licensed Function for an Authorised Person, the entity's auditor or audit team members, the DFSA, a criminal law enforcement agency in the UAE, and anyone else prescribed by the Rules. That list tells training designers exactly whom staff may approach.

Under Article 68A(4), the person "shall not be subject to any civil or contractual liability", no contractual or civil remedy can be enforced against them for the disclosure, and they must not be dismissed or subjected to action "reasonably likely to cause detriment" for making it. Article 68A(5) lets a Court order relief, and Article 68A(6) confirms that a whistleblower need not identify themselves to qualify.

sections.heading: What must an Authorised Person put in place under GEN 5.4?

blocks.text: An Authorised Person must have written, effective whistleblowing policies and procedures, review them periodically, and record every report. [GEN Rule 5.4.2](https://dfsaen.thomsonreuters.com/rulebook/gen-542) requires policies and procedures "to facilitate the reporting of regulatory concerns by whistleblowers" and "to assess and, where appropriate, escalate regulatory concerns reported to it", in writing, reviewed so they remain "appropriate, effective and up to date".

[GEN Rule 5.4.3](https://dfsaen.thomsonreuters.com/rulebook/gen-543) requires a written record of each regulatory concern reported by a whistleblower, "including appropriate details of the regulatory concern and the outcome of its assessment". GEN 5.4.1 defines a regulatory concern as a concern that the firm, an officer or employee, or an Affiliate has contravened DFSA-administered legislation or engaged in money laundering, fraud or other financial crime.

The [guidance under GEN 5.4.3](https://dfsaen.thomsonreuters.com/rulebook/gen-543-guidance) fills in the design. It expects proportionality, with "more detailed and comprehensive" arrangements for larger or more complex firms. Policies should provide internal reporting arrangements, escalation to senior management or the DFSA, confidentiality and identity protection, protection from detriment, feedback where feasible, and fair treatment of anyone accused. Firms should generally encourage internal reporting first while recognizing that a whistleblower may prefer to go directly to the DFSA.

sections.heading: Is whistleblowing training mandatory in the DIFC?

blocks.text: No rule prescribes a whistleblowing course as at November 2026, but the DFSA expects staff to be told about their protection, and the regime cannot work if they are not. Guidance 9 under GEN 5.4.3 states: "An Authorised Person should, as part of its whistleblowing policies and procedures, inform its officers and employees of the protection under Article 68A of the Regulatory Law."

Several other duties depend on trained people. Staff who receive reports must recognize a regulatory concern as defined in GEN 5.4.1, escalate it, keep it confidential, and record the seven items in Guidance 4. Managers must understand that Article 68A(4)(c) bars any detriment for a protected disclosure. GEN Rule 5.3.18 separately requires systems and controls that let the firm "satisfy itself of the suitability of anyone who acts for it".

blocks.title: Stated plainly
blocks.text: The DFSA Rules impose written policy, periodic review and record-keeping duties, and the guidance expects firms to inform staff of Article 68A. Neither the Regulatory Law nor GEN sets a training frequency, duration or curriculum. Annual refreshers are a design choice the firm must justify.

sections.heading: What protection does the DIFC Employment Law give?

blocks.text: The DIFC Employment Law protects against victimization only for acts connected with its non-discrimination Part 9. Article 60 of the [consolidated Employment Law](https://edge.sitecorecloud.io/dubaiintern0078-difcexperie96c5-production-3253/media/project/difcexperiences/difc/difcwebsite/documents/laws--regulations/employment-law.pdf) (Consolidated Version No. 5, July 2025) says "An Employer must not victimise an Employee", and lists protected acts such as bringing proceedings under Part 9, giving evidence, and alleging a contravention of Part 9. Article 60(3) removes protection for false allegations made in bad faith.

Two general provisions matter for training. Article 43(2) requires an employer to "provide and maintain a workplace that is free of discrimination and victimisation", with fines under Schedule 2. Article 54(2)(b) makes an employer liable for an employee's discrimination or victimization unless it can show it took "such steps as were reasonably practicable to prevent" it. Manager training on retaliation is one of the steps an employer would point to. For a financial whistleblower, the stronger protection is Article 68A of the Regulatory Law.

sections.heading: How should a DIFC firm build its whistleblowing training?

items: Confirm which entities are Authorised Persons subject to GEN 5.4 and which group policies they rely on.
Write the policy against GEN 5.4.2 and the six design points in Guidance 2, then build training from that policy rather than from a generic template.
Teach all staff what a regulatory concern is, the Article 68A(3) recipients, that anonymous reports are protected, and that detriment is prohibited.
Give report handlers a separate module on triage, escalation, confidentiality, and the seven-item record in Guidance 4.
Train people managers on retaliation risk, including the reasonably practicable steps defense in Employment Law Article 54(2)(b).
Retrain after each GEN 5.4.2(3) review that changes the policy, and keep the version history.

blocks.text: Related DIFC obligations are covered on [DFSA training and competence requirements](/regulations/dfsa-training-and-competence-requirements) and the [DIFC Data Protection Law training page](/regulations/difc-data-protection-law-training), which matters because whistleblowing records contain personal data. Industry context is on the [financial services](/industries/financial-services) page.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Article 68A, each GEN 5.4 Rule and its guidance, and the firm's own policy as linked obligations, with assessment points for staff, report handlers and managers. When the policy is revised after a periodic review, the affected modules and learners are identified from the changed clause.

faqs.q: Can a DIFC employee report directly to the DFSA?
faqs.a: Yes. The DFSA is one of the recipients listed in Article 68A(3), so a good faith disclosure to it is protected. The GEN 5.4.3 guidance says firms should generally encourage internal reporting first but must recognize that a whistleblower may prefer, or it may be appropriate, to report directly to the DFSA or another authority.

faqs.q: Are anonymous reports protected in the DIFC?
faqs.a: Yes. Article 68A(6) states that a person does not need to identify themselves when making a disclosure to qualify for protection. Firms should design reporting channels and training so that staff know anonymous routes exist and so that handlers know how to assess and record anonymous reports.

faqs.q: Must a DIFC firm report every whistleblowing concern to the DFSA?
faqs.a: GEN 5.4 does not require automatic onward reporting of every concern. It requires the firm to assess and, where appropriate, escalate, and Guidance 4(f) says the record should capture the outcome and any decision on whether to disclose the report to the DFSA or another authority. Guidance 5 adds that the DFSA may inspect whistleblowing records.

faqs.q: Does whistleblower protection stop a firm disciplining an employee?
faqs.a: Not for unrelated reasons. GEN 5.4.3 Guidance 8 explains that the protection is from liability, dismissal or detriment for making the disclosure, and does not prevent action for other legitimate reasons such as misconduct. Managers need training to separate the two and to document the reasons for any decision.
